turn_text: Well, thank you very much. It's great to be on with you.

There are acting negotiations on trade treaties going on right now in the Pacific Rim, the Transpacific Partnership, appears to have stalled in some talks with Japan. What are your views on that 12-nation trade agreement and whether Japan should be part of it?

Well, I do see opportunities to expand trade, expand markets for our producers here at home. I am very concerned that Japan wants to shut out U.S. agricultural products. I think they're a little protectionist in their views. So if they can't open up, I would have problems with Japan staying in the agreement. So we're working on that right now. I think it's important, though, that we keep people engaged as much as we can with all of the countries participating at this point. Let's make sure that we maintain the discussion. But we also need to establish expectations for Japan to open up opportunities for our for our producers to sell into that market.
What about a trade agreement with China? Do you think that's feasible?

Well, at this point, I don't want to get out there too far and reach for something that maybe isn't ready, I think, ultimately. We have some things that need to be ironed out in terms of China and trade. It's an important market. We know that their biotech approval system has been somewhat disruptive. A lot of our producers, I think, have just They know what to expect, perhaps, but they're shutting out our grain and that's a problem longer term. So I would hope that perhaps we could iron out to some of these challenges in the future.

On the Atlantic side, they have the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership, and there we're up against the European Union, which has been quite stubborn in modifying policies and accepting our U.S. agricultural products. Do you think those negotiations are heading in the right direction?

I see opportunities there again to iron out some of these challenges, especially how they treat our biotech products. Obviously, it's not based on science. And we want to take advantage of these opportunities to put science-based standards in so that the sanitary, phyto-sanitary issues can be addressed as well. So that we're all singing from the same hymnal, so to speak, and that we have an understanding that science-based standards are the way to go so the political games can't be played, whether it's biotech or, like I said, SPS. and other issues.
Now to make all this work, the president has to have some more authority, it appears. Are you prepared to give President Obama fast track authority on trade deals?

Well we want, we're looking right now at the Trade Priorities Act. This would tee up the system to move forward with trade agreements and it happens to be, you know, the Obama administration right now. We don't even yet know if we can get all these things lined up right away. But fact of the matter is, we need a system to negotiate aggressively and effectively on trade. And so we want to set up a process to make sure that Congress has the ultimate say. Constitutionally, it has to happen that way. So anything that would come up for a trade deal would have to come for a vote of Congress. We want to make sure that we're good negotiators, that we are strategic negotiators. I myself have been involved, for example, in the Columbia Trade Agreement a few years ago of raising some issues that needed to be addressed in the Trade Agreement. Got those things ironed out. And I think we've seen already some good results from past trade agreements. And when you look at the trade agreements with various countries that we've already engaged in, I think it's important to see the successes that have taken place. Now there is, you know, the fact that even top officials have acknowledged that it's difficult to move the Trans-Pacific Partnership or TTIP without the Trade Priorities Act. So we need to continue these discussions moving forward and make sure, though, that we maintain the prerogatives of Congress.

turn_text: Congressman, you're from a rural and definitely agricultural district. USDA is now attempting to implement the 2014 farm legislation. How do you think they're doing?

Well, I think it's still a little early to tell, but I know that efforts in terms of the disaster programs, there's been a concerted effort to make sure that the rollout for those programs are effective and useful. But I'm anxious to hear from producers themselves as we continue to see the rollout.
You're a co-chair of the modern agriculture caucus that has just been established
wonder you just had your first meeting. What is the focus of the group?

Well, the focus of the group I think is to really promote new ways of doing things in agriculture. We know that producers are always looking for new ways of doing things and being more efficient, more effective with their resources. Part of what I'm trying to do is tell the very positive story to my colleagues that we are seeing record yields and its droughts, perhaps over the last few years, we see record yields using less land, less water. These are some great narratives that I think generally the public doesn't always get to see or hear. So we're focusing on that. And boy, it's exciting when you see what has been done in the horizon. It looks very positive, too, in terms of newer technologies, whether it's biotech, whether it's new irrigation methods, whether there's a great story to tell. So we're using the modern ag caucus to highlight that. The issue that we've been working on is making sure that the facts are out there relating to animal welfare issues. We know that livestock America is what I call it, livestock America is not only helping feed our country, but it's helping feed the world. And we don't want to see unnecessary, perhaps a well-intentioned regulations, but unnecessary and counterproductive regulations take place in a way that would really actually hurt consumers. turn_text: Finally back home and the issue of property rights and energy regarding the Keystone XL pipeline that I believe passes through your district, definitely through Nebraska. What's your position on that pipeline and why do you think the president is taking so long to make any decision on building it?

I think the president is taking a long time. There are some some dueling constituencies. I think that the president has to deal with But when I look at it and studying it, I've taken obviously the opportunity to study this and I've arrived at the fact that I can support the pipeline. I think it is very possible to utilize today's technology with a new pipeline and protect the environment. We know that a pipeline in this situation is the safest way to transport the product, certainly safer than rail or highway. And I think that seeing what the possibilities are, it's time to get this done that I think the president has had enough time to study it. Obviously, many of the studies, well, all of the studies have pointed out to the fact that this cannon should be done in a responsible way. And we can ultimately end up with a better energy policy as part of this. And we know that not including municipal pipelines, but just across rural Nebraska, there's already some 8,000 miles of pipelines crisscrossing even in the Sandhills area, areas, I should say. So I think we can responsibly get this done, protect the environment, protect our natural resources, and end up getting some petroleum from a country friendly to us, I think. You know, when you talk about overall energy transportation, ethanol is important, and here we see rail capacity taken up with oil, and that I think puts grains and processed grains into ethanol at a competitive disadvantage because the transportation costs have been driven up.
